title: Priyadarshan Just Walked Out of Hera Pheri 3 — and Says the Film Will Never Be Made
excerpt: Two days after the producer promised it's coming 'very soon,' the director who made the original a classic says legal chaos and personal feuds have killed the sequel for good
body:
The most beloved comedy trio in Hindi cinema just shared a screen again. **Akshay Kumar**, **Suniel Shetty**, and **Paresh Rawal** turned up together in *Welcome To The Jungle*, and for a few glorious hours, it felt like the universe was finally aligning for the one film every desi audience has been demanding for two decades.


Then **Priyadarshan** opened his mouth and broke every heart in the diaspora.

"To the best of my knowledge, *Hera Pheri 3* will never hit the screen due to lots of legal issues and personal conflicts," the director told *HT City* on Sunday. "Whether I am involved or not is unimportant."

The statement landed like a slap — not least because producer **Firoz Nadiadwala** had said the exact opposite just forty-eight hours earlier. In an interview on Saturday, Nadiadwala told *Bollywood Hungama* that *Hera Pheri 3* was happening "very soon," and even teased a crossover film between the *Hera Pheri* and *Welcome* franchises. "We have lovable characters," he'd said, practically glowing. "Baburao, Raju, Shyam, Uday, Majnu — bring them together, and it works."

Two days later, the director of the original walks out and declares the whole thing dead on arrival.

## What Went Wrong


![Akshay Kumar — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2a/Akshay_Kumar_National_Award_for_Padman_%28cropped%29.jpg)



> **""To the best of my knowledge, *Hera Pheri 3* will never hit the screen due to lots of legal issues and personal conflicts," the director told *HT City* on Sunday."**



The mess behind *Hera Pheri 3* is a masterclass in how Bollywood can fumble a sure thing. Multiple parties are now fighting over who actually owns the franchise — and the answer is genuinely unclear.

The original *Hera Pheri* (2000) was a Hindi remake of the Malayalam cult classic *Ramji Rao Speaking*, produced by **Seven Arts International** out of Kerala. That production house has now taken Nadiadwala to court, arguing that he only had limited rights to make the Hindi version and violated their copyright by greenlighting the sequel *Phir Hera Pheri* and later transferring rights to Akshay Kumar's company, **Cape of Good Films**.

The case reached the **Madras High Court** in April 2026, where a judge rejected Nadiadwala's attempt to dismiss the complaint — ruling that questions about copyright, remake rights, and enforceability require a full trial. In plain terms: a court has said there's a genuine dispute over who owns Raju, Shyam, and Baburao.

And that's not even all of it. **Bhushan Kumar** of T-Series has publicly claimed ownership of the music rights, adding yet another layer to a franchise that now has more litigants than laughs.

## The Paresh Problem (That Wasn't)

Last May, news broke that Paresh Rawal had quit the project entirely — a story that sent fans into a spiral. Rawal eventually returned, and a *Bollywood Hungama* fact-check in May 2026 confirmed that reports of a second exit were recycled old news. But the incident revealed just how fragile the project's foundations have always been. Even the actors don't seem entirely sure what they've signed up for.


![Paresh Rawal — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d3/Paresh_Rawal_February_2015.jpg)


## Why This Stings for the Diaspora

There are films, and then there are cultural artefacts. *Hera Pheri* is the latter — a film that lives in group chats, wedding speeches, and every NRI house party where someone inevitably does a Baburao impression. For Indians abroad, quoting *Hera Pheri* is practically a citizenship test. *"Utha le re baba"* is not a line; it's an identity.

The sequel, *Phir Hera Pheri* (2006), divided opinion but kept the franchise alive in pop culture. A third instalment was supposed to reunite the original trio under Priyadarshan's direction — a full-circle moment for a generation that grew up on these films.

Instead, what they've got is a director saying it's dead, a producer saying it's happening, and a court deciding who gets to claim the characters.

> "What Feroze has said is true. I am not associated with Hera Pheri 3 at present." — Priyadarshan, to *Hindustan Times*

## So Is It Over?

Not necessarily. Nadiadwala is a producer who has survived worse legal tangles, and the commercial logic of *Hera Pheri 3* remains irresistible — the original still trends on social media regularly, and both sequels are among the most-rewatched comedies on Indian OTT platforms. The IP is too valuable to die quietly.

But without Priyadarshan — the man who understood the timing, the chaos, the peculiar alchemy of those three actors together — any version of *Hera Pheri 3* risks becoming what *Phir Hera Pheri* was accused of being: a copy that doesn't quite get the joke.

For now, Raju, Shyam, and Baburao remain frozen in 2000 and 2006, immortal in memes and WhatsApp forwards, waiting for a courtroom to decide if they'll ever get to be funny again.
